cues.text: Welcome to Plant Physiology, our NEET Biology Unit four foundation.
This recording uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Photosynthesis connects light capture with the formation of organic compounds
from inorganic carbon.
In the familiar oxygenic plant account, carbon dioxide supplies carbon, while
water supplies electrons and is the source of released oxygen.
A balanced summary equation does not show every intermediate or prove the
source of each atom.
The chloroplast envelope surrounds a stroma containing enzymes of carbon
fixation.
Thylakoid membranes carry photosystems and electron transport machinery, with
a
distinct internal lumen.
Grana are stacks of thylakoids connected by other thylakoid regions; a granum
is not an extra independent organelle.
Light reactions make ATP and reducing power that support biosynthetic
reactions.
Calling the Calvin cycle a dark reaction does not mean it normally operates
only at night.
Keep carbon movement, electron movement and energy transfer separate when
interpreting a diagram.
Chlorophyll a is central to the reaction centres of oxygenic photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll b and carotenoids contribute as accessory pigments, broadening
light absorption and, in suitable contexts, protecting against excess
excitation.
Pigments are organized with proteins in light harvesting complexes rather than
floating as one uniform green solution.
Antenna pigments transfer excitation energy toward a reaction centre; this is
different from claiming that the same electron travels through every antenna
pigment.
An absorption spectrum describes how strongly a pigment absorbs different
wavelengths.
An action spectrum describes the effectiveness of wavelengths in driving a
biological process such as photosynthesis.
The two are related but need not be identical because several pigments and
cellular processes contribute.
Blue and red light are strongly used in the familiar chlorophyll comparison;
green light is less strongly absorbed by an isolated chlorophyll sample, not
universally useless to an entire leaf.
Read the axes and the material being measured before comparing spectral
curves.
Photosystem two is named PSII but acts before photosystem one in the usual
linear electron flow.
Its reaction centre chlorophyll pair is designated P six eighty, referring to
a
characteristic absorption wavelength rather than a count of pigment molecules.
Light excitation supports charge separation and electron transfer to an
acceptor.
Electrons lost by the reaction centre are replaced through the water oxidizing
machinery.
Oxidation of water releases electrons, protons into the thylakoid lumen and
molecular oxygen.
This is why plant oxygen release must not be attributed to splitting carbon
dioxide.
Downstream carriers, including plastoquinone and the cytochrome complex in the
elementary scheme, connect PSII to PSI.
Energy changes along this path help build the proton gradient that supports
ATP
formation.
A diagram with an upward energy step represents light input rather than a
literal upward movement through the leaf.
Separate the source of electrons from the final destination of electrons and
from the compartment in which protons accumulate.
Photosystem one has a reaction centre designated P seven hundred.
In linear electron flow, electrons arriving from the earlier chain are
reenergized by light at PSI and transferred through carriers including
ferredoxin toward reduction of NADP plus to NADPH.
The complete linear pathway involves both photosystems, water oxidation and
oxygen release, and supports formation of ATP as well as NADPH.
In cyclic electron flow around PSI, electrons return through a carrier pathway
instead of producing a net transfer to NADP plus.
This can increase ATP production without net NADPH formation or oxygen
evolution attributable to that cyclic loop.
It does not require PSII water splitting as part of the loop itself.
Cyclic does not mean the ATP molecule travels back into a photosystem, and
noncyclic does not mean there are no repeated reactions anywhere in the
chloroplast.
The names describe the route of electrons.
Compare products and electron destinations rather than memorizing the word
cycle without specifying what cycles.
Chemiosmosis links a proton electrochemical gradient to ATP synthesis across a
membrane.
In a functioning chloroplast light reaction system, water oxidation supplies
lumenal protons and carrier mediated processes contribute to a higher proton
concentration in the lumen than in the stroma.
Reduction of NADP plus also draws on stromal protons in the elementary
account.
The thylakoid membrane limits unrestricted proton movement, maintaining the
difference.
Protons return toward the stroma through ATP synthase, whose catalytic
machinery forms ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.
The direction of proton return is essential: from lumen to stroma in this
chloroplast comparison.
ATP is not made merely because oxygen bubbles are present, nor does the
membrane have to rupture to let protons pass.
An uncoupling pathway can reduce ATP synthesis despite continued electron
transport.
Distinguish electron carriers, proton transfer and ATP synthase, and identify
the two membrane sides before comparing this mechanism with a mitochondrion.
The Calvin cycle has carboxylation, reduction and regeneration phases in the
chloroplast stroma.
RuBisCO catalyzes the addition of carbon dioxide to ribulose bisphosphate, or
RuBP.
The unstable six carbon intermediate gives two molecules of three
phosphoglycerate, called three PGA.
ATP and NADPH support conversion through later intermediates to triose
phosphate.
Most of this carbon is used to regenerate RuBP rather than leaving the cycle
immediately as a whole glucose molecule.
In the standard balance, fixation of three carbon dioxide molecules yields a
net one three carbon triose phosphate while consuming nine ATP and six NADPH.
A six carbon carbohydrate equivalent therefore requires twice that carbon
input
and energy accounting.
Regeneration matters because depletion of the acceptor would stop continued
fixation.
RuBisCO does not itself generate the light reaction ATP, and a three carbon
first stable product does not mean the initial carbon dioxide acceptor has
three carbons.
Follow carbon totals at each stage.
In the typical C four leaf account, initial fixation in mesophyll cells uses
phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, or PEP carboxylase, with bicarbonate as the
immediate inorganic carbon substrate.
The first stable product is oxaloacetate, a four carbon compound that can be
converted to other transport acids.
These compounds carry carbon toward bundle sheath cells, where decarboxylation
supplies a high carbon dioxide concentration around RuBisCO.
The Calvin cycle still operates there; C four plants have not replaced it with
a completely unrelated sugar making cycle.
The returning three carbon compound participates in regeneration of PEP at an
additional energy cost.
In the usual simplified comparison, this costs about two additional ATP
equivalents per carbon dioxide concentrated.
Maize and sugarcane are familiar examples with Kranz anatomy, though detailed
biochemical subtypes vary.
Carbon concentration reduces photorespiration and can favor performance under
suitable warm conditions.
Four carbon first product and five carbon Calvin acceptor describe different
stages, not contradictory descriptions of one molecule.
RuBisCO has both carboxylase and oxygenase activities.
In the oxygenase reaction, RuBP combines with oxygen to form one three
phosphoglycerate and one two phosphoglycolate, rather than two three carbon
Calvin products.
Processing the phosphoglycolate through photorespiratory metabolism involves
chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria in the standard plant account.
Carbon is partially recovered, but the pathway uses energy and releases some
previously fixed carbon dioxide; it is not an additional net sugar producing
alternative to the Calvin cycle.
A higher oxygen to carbon dioxide ratio around RuBisCO and suitable high
temperature conditions can favor this competition.
Stomatal closure can restrict carbon dioxide entry and intensify the issue.
C four carbon concentration suppresses photorespiration but does not prove
RuBisCO has lost its oxygenase capacity.
Photorespiration is different from ordinary mitochondrial respiration, even
though mitochondria participate.
The prefix photo identifies its connection with photosynthetic metabolism, not
a new method of making extra ATP from wasted carbon.
Photosynthetic rate depends on interacting external and internal factors.
Light intensity, carbon dioxide availability, temperature and water status
matter alongside pigment, enzyme and leaf characteristics.
A limiting factor is the factor currently restricting rate in a stated
situation.
Increasing a different factor may have little effect until the limitation
changes.
A light response curve often rises at low light and approaches saturation, but
sufficiently strong light can also cause damage or protective downregulation.
Temperature affects enzyme reactions and related processes, so an optimum is
context dependent rather than one universal temperature for every plant.
Water shortage can close stomata, restrict carbon dioxide entry and alter
metabolism; its effect is not captured only by counting water molecules in a
summary equation.
C three and C four plants can respond differently to carbon dioxide and
temperature, but neither label guarantees superiority in every environment.
In an experimental graph, change one variable carefully and identify the
factors being held constant.
A starch test can provide evidence of carbohydrate accumulation in a leaf, but
iodine does not directly detect carbon dioxide fixation, ATP synthesis or
oxygen evolution.
A previously destarched plant, suitable light exposure and appropriate
controls
help interpret the result.
A variegated leaf comparison asks how green and nongreen regions differ, while
controlled carbon dioxide availability investigates another requirement.
Boiling ethanol and other laboratory steps require supervised safe procedures;
this recording focuses on interpretation rather than unsupervised handling.
Gas exchange measurements record the net result of processes occurring
together.
In a lit leaf, photosynthetic carbon uptake can coexist with respiratory
carbon
release.
Net carbon assimilation is therefore less than gross uptake when opposing
losses are present.
At a stated compensation point, the measured opposing fluxes balance; this
does
not mean every enzyme and organelle has stopped.
Bubble counts can be influenced by temperature, gas dissolution and bubble
size, so they are an imperfect proxy for a precise photosynthetic rate.
Plant cells require respiration for usable chemical energy in both green and
nongreen tissues.
Roots, developing seeds and other nonphotosynthetic parts respire, while
photosynthetic cells also respire.
Plants do not have a vertebrate style lung and blood circulation system for
gas
delivery.
Gases can diffuse through stomata, lenticels and other surfaces, then through
intercellular spaces and short cellular distances.
The balance of photosynthetic and respiratory gas exchange changes with light,
tissue and conditions.
Saying plants release oxygen by day and carbon dioxide only at night is
therefore an overgeneralization; respiration continues in suitable living
cells
during the day as well.
Waterlogged soil can reduce oxygen availability around roots and constrain
aerobic metabolism even when a shoot has access to air.
Breathing, gas exchange and cellular respiration are related ideas but not
identical definitions.
The following pathways describe controlled chemical transfers of carbon and
electrons, rather than the simple physical movement of air into a leaf.
Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol and converts a six carbon glucose into
two three carbon pyruvate molecules through a sequence of enzyme catalyzed
steps.
An investment phase uses two ATP equivalents in the standard glucose account.
After splitting and interconversion of intermediates, both three carbon
branches contribute to the payoff reactions.
Four ATP are formed by substrate level phosphorylation, giving a net gain of
two ATP after the investment is subtracted.
Two NADH are also formed per glucose.
NAD plus must remain available for the oxidation step, so regeneration of this
carrier is important when oxygen supply or downstream metabolism is
restricted.
Glycolysis does not directly consume molecular oxygen and can occur in aerobic
as well as fermentative metabolism.
No carbon dioxide is released in the standard glucose to pyruvate sequence.
Gross ATP produced, net ATP gained and reduced carrier production are
different
quantities; do not add them together without stating how later carrier
oxidation is being accounted for.
When respiratory oxidation of NADH is insufficient, fermentation can
regenerate
NAD plus so that glycolysis continues.
In alcoholic fermentation, pyruvate first loses carbon dioxide to form
acetaldehyde, which is then reduced to ethanol using NADH.
Yeast is a familiar example, and some oxygen deprived plant tissues can also
produce ethanol.
In lactic fermentation, reduction of pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD plus
without the carbon dioxide releasing step.
These alternatives do not produce additional ATP in their conversion of
pyruvate in the standard account.
Their ATP yield is the net two ATP supplied by glycolysis per glucose.
Fermentation leaves substantial chemical energy in its organic end products,
so
it cannot be equated with complete oxidation to carbon dioxide and water.
Anaerobic respiration in some microorganisms, involving alternative terminal
electron acceptors, is a distinct concept from these elementary fermentation
pathways.
Always specify the organism, conditions and end product instead of assuming
every oxygen limited cell makes exactly the same substance.
For the usual aerobic eukaryotic pathway, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion
and
undergoes oxidative decarboxylation through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex
in the matrix.
A three carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as carbon dioxide, leaving a two
carbon acetyl group attached to coenzyme A.
NAD plus is reduced to NADH.
The direct products per pyruvate are therefore acetyl coenzyme A, one carbon
dioxide and one NADH, with no direct ATP production in this link step.
One glucose gives two pyruvates, so the link reaction totals must be doubled
per glucose.
Coenzyme A serves as an acetyl group carrier and is released when the group
enters the following cycle; it is not itself one of the two carbons being
oxidized.
This reaction links glycolysis with the citric acid cycle but should not be
silently counted twice when a question separately lists both stages.
Track the reference amount: per pyruvate and per glucose give different
numerical answers.
The tricarboxylic acid cycle, also called the citric acid or Krebs cycle,
begins with a two carbon acetyl group joining four carbon oxaloacetate to form
six carbon citrate.
A sequence of rearrangements, oxidations and decarboxylations regenerates
oxaloacetate.
The cycle does not consume a new oxaloacetate molecule irreversibly on every
turn.
In the standard balance per acetyl coenzyme A, it produces three NADH, one
FADH two, one substrate level ATP equivalent and two carbon dioxide molecules.
The ATP equivalent can be represented through GTP in a common biochemical
account.
Double these yields for the two acetyl groups derived from one glucose.
Most reactions are associated with the mitochondrial matrix, while succinate
dehydrogenase is an inner membrane enzyme that also participates in electron
transport.
Carbon dioxide loss over a turn does not require both incoming acetyl carbons
to be the first carbons released in that same turn.
Separate net cycle accounting from detailed tracing of a labeled carbon atom.
The mitochondrial electron transport system is associated with the inner
membrane.
Reduced carriers formed in earlier pathways transfer electrons into it.
In the familiar scheme, NADH donates through complex one, whereas succinate
associated electron transfer reaches the ubiquinone pool through complex two.
Mobile carriers and later complexes pass electrons toward molecular oxygen,
which is reduced to water at the terminal step.
Oxygen is therefore not directly required as a reactant in every glycolytic or
citric acid cycle reaction, but it is essential to the usual terminal
respiratory chain and continued efficient regeneration of oxidized carriers.
Complexes one, three and four support proton pumping in this standard chain;
complex two does not pump protons.
The resulting gradient stores part of the transferred energy rather than
converting all released energy directly into ATP in one chemical leap.
Plant mitochondria can have additional routes such as alternative oxidase, so
the basic diagram is a teaching scheme rather than every possible respiratory
electron pathway.
In mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, respiratory electron transfer
supports proton movement from the matrix toward the intermembrane space.
The inner membrane restricts unrestricted proton return.
Protons move back toward the matrix through ATP synthase, coupling that flow
to
phosphorylation of ADP.
This compartmental direction differs from the chloroplast lumen to stroma
comparison, even though both systems use chemiosmosis.
The catalytic part of mitochondrial ATP synthase faces the matrix in the
elementary account.
Substrate level phosphorylation is different: an enzyme transfers a phosphate
from a suitable metabolic intermediate to ADP or a related nucleotide without
requiring this membrane gradient.
An uncoupler allows the gradient to dissipate and can lower ATP yield even
while electron flow and oxygen use continue.
Blocking electron transport is therefore not identical to uncoupling it.
Distinguish the energy source, the membrane sides and the site of nucleotide
phosphorylation before predicting what a particular inhibitor or membrane leak
would change.
A single universal ATP total for every respiring cell is misleading.
In the standard complete glucose balance, glycolysis, the link reaction and
two
cycle turns together provide ten NADH, two FADH two and four substrate level
ATP equivalents.
An older idealized textbook convention assigns three ATP per NADH and two per
FADH two, giving thirty eight ATP before accounting for complications.
Contemporary approximate ratios of two point five and one point five instead
give thirty two with favorable handling of cytosolic reducing equivalents;
different shuttle arrangements can lower this to about thirty.
Real yields also depend on transport costs, proton leak, substrate use and
other pathways.
Plant mitochondrial alternative electron routes can change coupling further.
For an examination calculation, use the explicit assumptions provided and
label
the convention rather than silently mixing ratios from different models.
A theoretical total is not a measurement of every ATP molecule a living leaf
actually produces from each glucose.
Respiration is commonly introduced as the breakdown of organic substrates, but
its pathways also supply precursors for biosynthesis.
This dual involvement in degradation and synthesis is described as amphibolic.
Acetyl coenzyme A connects carbohydrate oxidation with fatty acid metabolism,
while citric acid cycle intermediates can contribute carbon skeletons for
amino
acid and other cellular synthesis.
Amino acids may enter respiratory pathways after appropriate removal or
transfer of nitrogen and conversion to suitable intermediates.
They do not all enter at exactly the same point.
Glycerol can feed carbohydrate related pathways after suitable
transformations,
while fatty acids are commonly broken down to acetyl units through beta
oxidation.
When intermediates are withdrawn for synthesis, their supply must be
maintained
by other reactions for continued cycle function.
Thus the diagram should be read as a network with exchanges, not an isolated
pipe that only accepts glucose and only releases waste.
Amphibolic does not mean a cell is simultaneously synthesizing and degrading
the same molecule at equal rates.
The respiratory quotient, or RQ, is the ratio of carbon dioxide released to
oxygen consumed during the stated respiratory process.
Comparable molar amounts or gas volumes under the same conditions can be used.
Complete oxidation of glucose releases six carbon dioxide while consuming six
oxygen, giving RQ one.
Fats require relatively more oxygen for their carbon oxidation and typically
give a value below one, often near zero point seven.
Some organic acids can give values above one.
Mixed substrates, incomplete oxidation and gas exchange complications require
care, so RQ alone is not an infallible identification of one nutrient in every
living tissue.
In alcoholic fermentation, carbon dioxide may be released without oxygen
consumption; dividing by zero does not give an ordinary finite aerobic RQ.
A whole green leaf under light also has photosynthetic gas fluxes, so an
uncorrected net gas ratio may not measure respiratory RQ.
Write the numerator and denominator before substituting numbers, especially
when a question reverses their order.
Seed germination involves renewed growth of the embryo under suitable
conditions.
Imbibition allows dry tissues to take up water, enzyme activity resumes and
stored reserves support early development.
Water, appropriate temperature and adequate oxygen are important for many
terrestrial seeds, while light requirements vary among species.
A seed under water can receive water yet lack sufficient oxygen, so one
favorable factor does not guarantee successful germination.
Radicle emergence is a common operational marker for germination, and seedling
establishment continues beyond that point.
A viable seed can remain dormant because of internal constraints even when
several external conditions appear suitable.
Dormancy is different from death and from simple quiescence caused only by
currently unfavorable surroundings.
Protective coats, embryo state and regulator balance can contribute in
different species.
Germination does not require the seed to photosynthesize before it uses stored
reserves.
Distinguish the embryo, its reserve tissues and the environmental conditions
when interpreting why a particular treatment changes the response.
Plant growth is an irreversible increase in size, commonly accompanied by
increases in dry mass, cell number or related measures depending on the system
being studied.
Temporary swelling from water uptake alone should not automatically be equated
with sustained developmental growth.
In a growing root, a meristematic region contains actively dividing cells, an
elongation region shows substantial cell expansion and a maturation region
develops specialized functions such as root hair formation.
These regions are related stages in a spatial pattern, not separate species of
cells fixed for the entire life of the plant.
A finite organ often shows a sigmoid growth curve with an initial lag, faster
growth and a slowing or stationary phase as limitations develop.
Whole plant growth can be more complex because new organs and meristems
continue to contribute.
Length, area, volume, fresh mass and dry mass are different measurements; a
treatment can change one without proportionally changing every other measure.
An arithmetic growth model adds equal absolute increments in equal time
intervals, producing a straight line under its stated assumptions.
A geometric or exponential model makes the increase proportional to the
existing size while resources remain unrestricted.
Living organs often depart from either simple model as conditions and
developmental programs change.
Absolute growth rate compares the actual increase in a measured quantity over
time.
Relative growth rate relates growth to the amount of material already present;
precise continuous calculations use logarithmic change over time.
A leaf increasing from five to ten square centimetres and another from fifty
to
fifty five each gain five square centimetres, yet the first has a much larger
proportional increase.
Thus equal absolute growth does not imply equal relative growth.
Always state the time interval and units.
A steeper graph can reflect the axis scale, and a percentage gain should not
be
compared with a length gain as though they were the same variable.
Growth depends on the interaction of genetic programs with environmental
conditions.
Water supports turgor driven expansion and metabolic reactions, minerals
provide essential materials, and appropriate temperature and oxygen
availability support suitable enzyme and respiratory activity.
Light affects both energy supply and developmental signaling, so a light
response is not always just a change in photosynthetic carbon fixation.
A dark grown seedling may elongate rapidly using reserves while showing a
pale,
unusual form; greater length alone does not establish healthier overall
development.
Nutrient or oxygen shortage can restrict growth even when water is abundant.
Plasticity refers to the capacity to show different forms or developmental
responses under different conditions or life stages.
Heterophylly, with different leaf forms in a plant's developmental or
environmental contexts, provides a familiar example.
Plasticity does not mean the environment rewrites every inherited sequence
whenever a leaf changes shape.
Use controlled comparisons to separate changes in growth rate, tissue
differentiation and the overall developmental pattern.
Differentiation is the process by which cells acquire specialized structural
and functional features.
Development of a tracheary element, for example, includes major wall
modification and eventual loss of living contents in the mature conducting
cell.
Not all differentiated cells follow that same route.
In suitable plant contexts, some living differentiated cells can regain the
ability to divide, a process called dedifferentiation.
Formation of an interfascicular cambium from appropriate parenchymatous cells
is a familiar textbook example.
The descendants can later specialize again through redifferentiation,
producing
cells with new functions.
This does not mean every dead plant cell can become a new meristem or that
every cell reverses its history spontaneously.
Development combines growth, division, differentiation and the arrangement of
tissues over time.
The same genotype can support different cellular roles through regulated
expression and environment.
Keep the capacity of a cell, the actual conditions triggering a response and
the fate of its descendants separate when interpreting a regeneration example.
Auxins are growth regulators with effects that depend on tissue, concentration
and developmental context.
Indole acetic acid, or IAA, is a familiar natural auxin.
Auxin signaling can promote cell elongation in suitable shoot tissues, while
roots often respond to lower concentrations and may be inhibited at
concentrations that stimulate shoots.
Differential auxin distribution contributes to tropic growth responses, so
uniform stimulation of every cell is not the explanation for bending.
Apical dominance involves signaling from the shoot apex and interactions with
other regulators; it is not proof that lateral buds lack living meristems.
Auxins are used in appropriate contexts to encourage adventitious rooting and
can influence fruit development and abscission responses.
Synthetic compounds such as NAA and two four D have different applications and
concentration dependent effects, including selective herbicidal use of the
latter.
Listing an application does not make it a safe universal treatment
recommendation.
In questions, identify the plant part and concentration before deciding
whether
an auxin promotes or suppresses growth.
Gibberellins are a group of plant growth regulators, with gibberellic acid or
GA three as a familiar example.
They can promote stem and internode elongation in responsive plants and induce
bolting, the rapid elongation associated with flowering in certain rosette
plants.
An increase in stem length does not mean every tissue has divided at the same
rate.
During germination in the familiar cereal model, gibberellin signaling from
the
embryo stimulates responses in the aleurone layer, including production of
enzymes that mobilize stored food.
This connects a regulator with reserve use rather than claiming the hormone
itself is the seed's food.
Gibberellins can also influence dormancy, fruit development and agricultural
traits in suitable species.
Their effects interact with other signals, including the generally contrasting
dormancy related action of ABA.
A response observed in one variety under one condition cannot be extended
automatically to every plant or organ.
Distinguish the regulator, the responding tissue and the downstream enzyme or
growth process.
Cytokinins are regulators associated with promotion of cell division in
suitable contexts, particularly when other growth requirements and signals are
present.
Zeatin is a familiar naturally occurring example.
Cytokinin effects include support for lateral bud outgrowth and delayed
senescence of some tissues, but these are regulated responses rather than a
promise that any leaf remains green forever.
Roots are important sites of cytokinin production in the elementary account,
while other tissues can also contribute.
Auxin and cytokinin balance is a useful framework for interpreting many tissue
culture responses.
In a classic responsive callus system, relatively more cytokinin can favor
shoot formation and relatively more auxin can favor root formation, with
intermediate conditions supporting callus growth.
This is an experimental pattern, not a universal numerical recipe for every
species and medium.
Nutrients, explant state and other regulators matter as well.
Compare relative concentrations and observed outcomes rather than treating one
hormone as the sole independent controller of all plant development.
Ethylene is a gaseous plant regulator produced in varied developmental and
stress contexts.
In climacteric fruits it promotes ripening and is associated with
characteristic changes in respiration, texture and other traits.
This should not be converted into a claim that every fruit has the same
ripening pattern or that every color change is caused only by ethylene.
Ethylene can promote senescence and abscission in suitable contexts and
interacts with auxin in the regulation of organ shedding.
A classic seedling triple response includes reduced elongation, increased
radial swelling and altered horizontal growth under the appropriate
experimental conditions.
Thus a plant regulator can restrict elongation while promoting another growth
response.
Ethephon can release ethylene and has regulated agricultural uses, but a
classroom example is not an instruction to apply chemicals without appropriate
controls.
Because ethylene is gaseous, enclosed environments can affect its accumulation
and responses.
Distinguish the chemical signal, its source, the exposure conditions and the
developmental competence of the target tissue.
Abscisic acid, abbreviated ABA, participates in seed maturation and dormancy
related programs and in responses to environmental stress.
During water deficit, ABA signaling promotes stomatal closure through changes
in guard cell ion transport and turgor, helping limit water loss.
This response can also reduce carbon dioxide entry, so water conservation and
photosynthetic rate can trade off under the stated conditions.
ABA is often described as a growth inhibiting regulator in elementary
comparisons, but this is a useful tendency rather than a complete account of
every dose, tissue and developmental response.
Its name does not mean it is the sole or universal cause of leaf abscission;
ethylene and interactions with other signals are important in many such
events.
Germination decisions can reflect the balance between ABA related dormancy
maintenance and gibberellin related responses, alongside environment and seed
state.
Avoid the shortcut that a stress hormone is always harmful: a response that
slows growth can contribute to survival under unfavorable conditions.
Plant development integrates growth, differentiation and transitions such as
germination, flowering and senescence.
Regulators interact with one another and with light, temperature, nutrients
and
water status.
Photoperiodic and temperature related responses provide useful context: a
developmental signal can depend on the pattern or duration of conditions
rather
than their effect on photosynthetic rate alone.
These contextual examples do not replace the explicitly prescribed Unit four
regulator and growth headings.
In an experiment, include a suitable untreated or vehicle control, hold other
variables comparable and distinguish a concentration response from a simple
claim that more hormone is always better.
Repeated observations and an appropriate time course help separate a transient
change from sustained development.
This recording provides foundations in photosynthesis, respiration and growth
against the dated official syllabus.
It includes the main carbon, energy, compartment and regulator comparisons,
but
further mixed graphs, inhibitor problems, experimental interpretation and
detailed pathway practice remain.
Continue by explaining a mechanism and its assumptions, rather than memorizing
an isolated product or hormone label.
